questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. The following. A list of 9 nodes indexed 0..8 has its tail linked back to the node at index 3. Using Floyd's slow/fast pointers, at which index do they first meet?

options.misconception: off by one from counting the first repeated visit
reports the tail that closes the cycle instead of the meeting node
reports the cycle entry point rather than the meeting point

questions.explanation: Simulating the pointers: slow advances one node and fast advances two each step until both land on index 6. The meeting point differs from the cycle entry at index 3, which is why confusing the two is a frequent error.
questions.hint: Advance slow once and fast twice per step, wrapping the tail to the cycle start, and watch for equality.

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. The values 66, 77, 88, 33, 11, 22, 55 are pushed onto an empty stack in that order, then 2 pop operations are performed. In what order are the values popped?

options.misconception: reverses the bottom k values instead of the top k
treats the stack like a queue and pops the earliest pushed values
pops in push order instead of reversing the top k values

questions.explanation: A stack is last-in first-out, so the 2 pops return the top 2 values in reverse push order: 55, 22. Reading them in push order or taking the bottom of the stack are the queue-style mistakes here.
questions.hint: The most recently pushed value always comes off first.

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. The values 60, 24, 48, 72, 36, 84 are enqueued into an empty queue in that order, then 2 dequeue operations are performed. In what order are the values removed?

options.misconception: reverses the first k values when they should keep insertion order
treats the queue like a stack and dequeues the newest values
dequeues the last values in push order instead of the first ones

questions.explanation: A queue is first-in first-out, so the 2 removals return the earliest enqueued values in order: 60, 24. Taking the newest values would be stack behavior, not queue behavior.

reverses the removal order of the two ends
lists values still in the deque as if they were removed

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. Evaluate the postfix expression "5 5 * 6 +" using a stack. What value remains?

options.misconception: multiplies everything and ignores operator precedence in postfix
adds all numbers and ignores the operator symbols
adds one from a misplaced counter

questions.explanation: Reading left to right, each operator pops its two most recent operands and pushes the result, ending with a single value 31. Treating the expression as infix or folding all numbers with one operator ignores how the stack defers operands.

counts every possible slot in the tree rather than only the occupied nodes
omits the root or one boundary node

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. Inserting 80, 75, 70, 65, 60, 90 (in that order) into an empty binary search tree, what is the parent of the node with value 75?

picks a value in the same subtree rather than tracing the search path
reports the target or a child instead of its parent

questions.explanation: Following the search rule, value 75 is placed under node 80: each comparison sends it left when smaller and right when larger. Values that are merely nearby in insertion order are not necessarily its parent.

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. Work out the requested value. In a binary heap stored in a zero-based array of 22 elements, what is the array index of the parent of index 8?

options.misconception: uses zero-based child or parent formulas that ignore the root offset
swaps the left and right child formulas
confuses a parent index with a child index

questions.explanation: With a zero-based array the parent of index i is floor((i-1)/2) and the children are 2i+1 and 2i+2. For i = 8 the requested parent index is 3. Shifting by one confuses this layout with a one-based array.
questions.hint: Start indexing at zero: the root is 0, its children are 1 and 2.

questions.stem: In a research synopsis, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. A min-heap has array representation 27, 31, 35, 15, 3. After inserting value 9 and sifting up as needed, what is the resulting array?

options.misconception: appends the value without restoring the heap order upward
reverses the whole array instead of sifting one element
places the new value at the root without comparing it to its parent

questions.explanation: The new value is appended at index 5 then swapped with its parent while it is smaller; the restored array is 9, 31, 27, 15, 3, 35. Skipping the sift or reversing the array breaks the min-heap property.
questions.hint: Append at the end, then repeatedly swap with the parent while it is smaller.

questions.stem: At a design critique, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. Applying bottom-up heapify to build a min-heap from the array 10, 5, 1, 2, 8, 7, what is the resulting array representation?

options.misconception: reverses the input rather than applying bottom-up heapify
fully sorts the array instead of only building a heap
builds a max-heap ordering instead of the requested min-heap

questions.explanation: Bottom-up heapify calls sift-down from the last internal node back to the root, producing a valid min-heap 1, 2, 7, 5, 8, 10; it does not fully sort the array. Each node is sifted only as far as needed.
questions.hint: Start at the last non-leaf index and sift down toward the root.

questions.stem: In a fieldwork record, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. Apply your knowledge to the following. Items (priority,value) (3,A) (4,C) (2,D) (5,E) (1,B) are inserted into a min-priority queue and then all are dequeued. In what order do the values leave?

options.misconception: uses a max-priority order instead of the requested min-priority order
dequeues in insertion order and ignores priorities entirely
outputs priority numbers instead of the stored values

questions.explanation: A min-priority queue returns the smallest priority first, using insertion or label order to break ties, so the values leave as B, D, A, C, E. Ignoring priorities or flipping to a max order are the two opposite mistakes here.
questions.hint: Sort by priority from smallest to largest, keeping ties stable.

questions.stem: During a bench check, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. Using the hash function h(k) = k mod m with table size m = 7, what bucket index does key 9 map to?

options.misconception: uses m-1 as the modulus instead of the table size m
doubles the key before hashing rather than using it directly
performs integer division instead of taking the remainder

questions.explanation: The remainder of 9 divided by 7 is 2, so that is the bucket index. Division or a wrong modulus gives a different bucket and is a common slip in hand-computed hashes.
questions.hint: Divide the key by the table size and keep only the remainder.

questions.stem: Review the following and respond. Keys 89, 105, 12, 25, 53, 64 are inserted into a hash table of size 13 using h(k)=k mod m and linear probing. At which array index does key 105 finally reside?

options.misconception: off by one in the probe sequence
reports the home bucket and ignores linear probing after a collision
reports insertion order rather than the final array index

questions.explanation: Inserting in order and probing forward on each collision places key 105 at index 1. Its home bucket is 1, so if that was occupied the probing sequence mattered. Reporting the home bucket is the classic mistake here.
questions.hint: Insert keys one at a time; when a slot is full, move to the next index with wraparound.

adds one from counting the empty chain
reports the number of buckets themselves

questions.learningObjective: demonstrate understanding of load factor & rehashing
questions.stem: In a review packet, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. A hash table of capacity 32 currently stores 15 entries. What is its load factor, rounded to two decimals?

options.misconception: subtracts one from the capacity as if one slot were reserved
inverts the ratio and divides capacity by the number of entries
uses the doubled capacity before rehashing actually occurs

questions.explanation: Load factor is entries divided by capacity, 15/32 = 0.47. It stays below 1 until rehashing, and an inverted ratio would no longer measure how full the table is.
questions.hint: Divide the number of stored entries by the table capacity.

omits one edge or neighbor

options.misconception: reverses the discovery order
rotates the start vertex to the end
uses breadth-first search instead

questions.explanation: DFS uses a stack (or recursion) and follows a path as deep as possible before backtracking. Starting at 2, the visit order is 2 -> 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5; the other option is the opposite traversal strategy.

questions.stem: During a process walkthrough, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. Here is a scenario to evaluate. In the unweighted connected graph 0:[1,2], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[0,1,4], 3:[1,4,5], 4:[2,3,5], 5:[3,4], how many edges are on a shortest path from vertex 0 to vertex 5?

options.misconception: assumes an unreachable target when the graph is connected
counts vertices on the path instead of edges
off by one in the level count

questions.explanation: In an unweighted graph a BFS from 0 discovers 5 at level 3, which is the number of edges on the shortest path. A path with 3 edges has 4 vertices, which is why counting vertices is the frequent slip.
questions.hint: Run BFS from the source and read off the level at which the target is discovered.

questions.stem: The case below gives the figures. Evaluate the following carefully. Using Kruskal's algorithm on the weighted edges [0-1:4, 0-2:2, 1-2:1, 1-3:5, 2-3:8, 2-4:10, 3-4:2, 3-5:6, 4-5:3], what is the total weight of a minimum spanning tree?

options.misconception: adds one extra edge weight
takes the five cheapest edges without skipping cycles
adds every edge weight instead of selecting the spanning tree

questions.explanation: Sorting edges by weight and accepting an edge only when it joins two different components gives a spanning tree of total weight 13. Adding every edge, or the five cheapest without cycle checks, overshoots because it keeps redundant edges.
questions.hint: Process edges cheapest first and skip any edge whose endpoints are already connected.

questions.stem: In a data memo, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. After one pass of insertion sort on the array 9, 5, 1, 3, 2, 6, what is the array state?

options.misconception: assumes a single pass fully sorts the whole array
applies the wrong rearrangement for this pass
leaves the array unchanged as if no pass occurred

questions.explanation: One pass of insertion sort moves only the element being placed in that pass; the prefix it touches becomes ordered but the rest stays as before, yielding 5, 9, 1, 3, 2, 6. Thinking the whole array is sorted after one pass is a common misconception.
questions.hint: Simulate exactly one outer-loop iteration, not the entire sort.

questions.stem: At a case conference, a coordinator summarizes the evidence: The case below gives the figures. Counting sort is applied to the digit array 4, 1, 0, 5, 0 with values in 0..5. What is the sorted output?

rotates the sorted output by one position
expands the counts in descending order instead of ascending

questions.explanation: counting sort tallies each digit then expands the counts in ascending order. Counting sort runs in O(n+k) time, and reading a count slot is different from reading the sorted output array.
questions.hint: Tally occurrences of each digit in 0..5 first, then read the requested quantity.

questions.stem: Use the facts presented to decide. Which comparison sort is stable and runs in O(n log n) worst case?

options.misconception: quick sort is not stable because partitioning swaps equal keys
selection sort is O(n^2) and swaps equal keys
heap sort is not stable because heapify reorders equal keys

questions.explanation: Merge sort fits all the stated constraints; each alternative fails one of them, whether stability, worst-case time, or auxiliary space. Matching every clause of the question to a known property avoids picking a sort that satisfies only part of it.
questions.hint: Check stability, worst-case time, and space separately for each candidate.
